lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: Mercury amalgamation is a method used by small-scale gold miners across Africa to capture fine gold from crushed ore or concentrates. It works because mercury binds with gold particles to form an amalgam, a soft, silvery-gold blob. This method is popular because it is cheap, fast, and requires little equipment. In many African countries like Ghana, Tanzania, Zimbabwe, and Burkina Faso, miners use mercury in sluice boxes, pans, or small ball mills. For example, a miner might add 10 grams of mercury to a bucket of concentrate and stir for 20 minutes. The amalgam is then squeezed through a cloth to remove excess mercury, leaving a hard ball that is later burned to evaporate the mercury, leaving raw gold. However, mercury is highly toxic. It damages the brain, kidneys, and lungs, and it never breaks down in the environment. When burned, it becomes an invisible vapor that can be inhaled by families, including children. In water, bacteria convert it to methylmercury, which builds up in fish and can poison entire communities. Despite these dangers, many miners continue because they lack safer alternatives or training. This module will teach you the correct techniques to minimize risk, but more importantly, it will show you why you should consider moving away from mercury altogether. You will learn how to use it safely if you must, but also how to protect yourself, your family, and your community. By the end, you will understand the full process, common mistakes, and best practices. Remember: mercury is not just a toolâit is a poison. Treat it with extreme respect.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To do mercury amalgamation safely and effectively, you need the right tools and materials. First, you need mercury itself. In Africa, it is often sold in small plastic bottles or syringes at mining supply shops. A typical amount is 100 grams, which costs about $10â$20 USD depending on the country. You also need a clean, non-porous container for mixingâa plastic bucket or a glass bowl works well. Avoid using aluminum or zinc containers because mercury reacts with them. You will need a sturdy stirring rod, preferably plastic or wood, not metal. For squeezing the amalgam, get a clean cotton cloth or a piece of chamois leather. A small rubber squeezer or a syringe without a needle can help remove excess mercury. For burning the amalgam, you need a retort or a fume hood. A simple retort can be made from a metal pipe and a condenser, but it is better to buy a proper one from a supplier. If you cannot get a retort, you must burn outdoors away from people and use a fan to blow vapors away. You also need personal protective equipment: nitrile gloves (not latex), safety goggles, and a respirator with a mercury vapor cartridge. A plastic apron is also good. For weighing, a small digital scale (0.1 g accuracy) helps measure mercury and gold. For storing mercury, use a sealed glass or plastic container with a tight lid, kept in a cool, dark place. Never store mercury in open containers or near food. Finally, have a spill kit ready: sulfur powder, a plastic scoop, and a sealed waste container. Sulfur binds with mercury to make it safer to clean up. All these tools should be kept away from children and animals. In many African mining communities, these items are available at local hardware stores or through mining cooperatives. If you cannot afford a retort, at least use a fume hood or burn outside. Your health is worth the investment.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps carefully to amalgamate gold with mercury. First, prepare your work area. Choose a well-ventilated spot outdoors, away from homes, children, and animals. Lay down a plastic sheet to catch spills. Put on your gloves, goggles, and respirator. Second, concentrate your gold. Mercury works best on fine, clean gold particles. Pan or sluice your ore to remove as much dirt and sand as possible. You want a heavy concentrate. Third, measure your mercury. A good ratio is 1 part mercury to 1 part gold by weight. For example, if you expect 5 grams of gold, use about 5 grams of mercury. Too much mercury makes the amalgam soft and hard to squeeze; too little leaves gold behind. Fourth, mix. Put your concentrate in a plastic bucket. Add the mercury. Add a small amount of water to cover the material. Stir gently but thoroughly for 15â20 minutes. The mercury will form a silvery paste with the gold. You will see the amalgam as a shiny, heavy blob. Fifth, separate the amalgam. Pour off the water and lighter material. The amalgam will settle at the bottom. Use your hands (with gloves) to pick up the amalgam. Sixth, squeeze. Put the amalgam in a cotton cloth. Twist the cloth tightly to squeeze out excess mercury. Do this over a container to catch the mercury. Keep squeezing until the amalgam is a hard, silver-gold ball. Seventh, burn. This is the most dangerous step. Place the amalgam in a retort or on a metal plate. Heat it with a torch or over a fire. The mercury evaporates, leaving gold. If using a retort, the mercury vapor is captured and can be reused. If not, do it outdoors with a fan blowing vapors away from you. Never breathe the fumes. Eighth, cool and weigh your gold. After burning, you have a sponge-like gold button. Melt it in a crucible to get pure gold. Remember: always work with a partner, and never eat, drink, or smoke during the process.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Many miners make mistakes that reduce gold recovery or increase mercury poisoning. Here are the most common ones and how to fix them. Mistake 1: Using too much mercury. This makes the amalgam runny and hard to squeeze, and you lose gold in the excess mercury. Fix: Use only 1:1 ratio of mercury to expected gold. Weigh if possible. Mistake 2: Not cleaning the concentrate. Dirty ore coats gold particles and prevents mercury from touching them. Fix: Pan or sluice your material until it is mostly black sand and gold. Mistake 3: Stirring too little or too little water. Mercury needs water to move freely and contact gold. Fix: Add enough water to cover the material and stir for at least 15 minutes. Mistake 4: Squeezing with bare hands. Mercury absorbs through skin. Fix: Always wear nitrile gloves. Mistake 5: Burning without a retort or in a closed room. This releases toxic vapor that you and your family inhale. Fix: Use a retort or burn outdoors with a fan. Never burn indoors. Mistake 6: Storing mercury in open containers. It evaporates at room temperature. Fix: Keep mercury in a sealed glass or plastic bottle. Mistake 7: Not cleaning up spills. Small mercury beads can hide in cracks and continue to vaporize. Fix: Use sulfur powder on spills. It turns mercury into a black compound that is less dangerous. Sweep it up and put it in a sealed container. Mistake 8: Letting children play with mercury. It looks like a shiny toy. Fix: Keep all mercury and amalgam away from children. Educate your family about the dangers. Mistake 9: Reusing mercury without filtering. Dirty mercury works poorly. Fix: Filter mercury through a fine cloth or coffee filter before reuse. Mistake 10: Ignoring health symptoms. Tremors, memory loss, and mouth sores are signs of mercury poisoning. Fix: See a doctor immediately and stop using mercury. By avoiding these mistakes, you will get more gold and stay healthier. Remember, mercury is a cumulative poisonâsmall exposures add up over time.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Mercury is one of the most toxic metals on Earth. It attacks the nervous system, kidneys, and lungs. In Africa, many miners suffer from mercury poisoning because they do not take safety seriously. This lesson will teach you best practices to protect yourself and your community. First, always wear personal protective equipment (PPE). This includes nitrile gloves (not latex, which mercury passes through), safety goggles, and a respirator with a mercury vapor cartridge. A simple dust mask is not enough. Second, work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. Mercury vapor is heavier than air and can accumulate in low places. Use a fan to blow vapors away from you. Never work in a closed room or near sleeping areas. Third, use a retort. A retort captures mercury vapor and turns it back into liquid mercury, which you can reuse. This saves money and prevents pollution. If you cannot afford a retort, burn outdoors away from people and animals. Fourth, never eat, drink, or smoke while working with mercury. Wash your hands and face thoroughly with soap and water after handling mercury, even if you wore gloves. Fifth, store mercury safely. Keep it in a sealed glass or plastic container, labeled clearly. Store away from food, water, and children. Sixth, clean up spills immediately. Use sulfur powder to bind mercury, then sweep it into a sealed container. Never use a vacuum cleanerâit spreads mercury vapor. Seventh, dispose of mercury waste properly. Never pour mercury down a drain or into a river. Collect waste in a sealed container and take it to a hazardous waste facility if available. In many African countries, mining cooperatives or NGOs can help with safe disposal. Eighth, educate your family and community. Mercury poisoning affects everyone, especially children and pregnant women. Methylmercury builds up in fish, so avoid eating fish from contaminated waters. Ninth, consider alternatives. There are mercury-free methods like gravity separation, borax smelting, or direct smelting. These are safer and increasingly affordable. Tenth, monitor your health. If you experience tremors, memory problems, or mouth sores, see a doctor and stop using mercury. Best practice is to stop using mercury altogether. But if you must use it, follow these rules strictly. Your life and your community's health depend on it.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: This practical exercise will help you practice mercury amalgamation safely and effectively. You will need: 10 grams of mercury, 10 grams of gold concentrate (or clean gold flakes), a plastic bucket, a stirring rod, a cotton cloth, nitrile gloves, safety goggles, a respirator, a digital scale, and a retort or outdoor burning area. Work outdoors away from people. Step 1: Put on your PPE. Gloves, goggles, and respirator. Step 2: Weigh 10 grams of mercury and 10 grams of gold concentrate. If you don't have a scale, use a small syringe to measure mercury (10 grams is about 0.74 mL). Step 3: Place the concentrate in the bucket. Add enough water to cover it. Add the mercury. Step 4: Stir gently for 20 minutes. You will see the mercury turn into a silvery paste. Step 5: Pour off the water and lighter material. The amalgam will settle at the bottom. Step 6: Pick up the amalgam with gloved hands. Put it in the cotton cloth. Step 7: Twist the cloth tightly to squeeze out excess mercury. Collect the mercury in a container for reuse. Keep squeezing until the amalgam is a hard ball. Step 8: Weigh the amalgam. It should weigh about 15â18 grams (gold plus some mercury). Step 9: Burn the amalgam. If you have a retort, use it. If not, place the amalgam on a metal plate and heat it with a torch outdoors, with a fan blowing vapors away. The mercury will evaporate, leaving a gold button. Step 10: Cool and weigh the gold. You should recover about 9â10 grams of gold. Step 11: Clean up. Use sulfur powder on any spills. Put waste in a sealed container. Wash your hands and face. Step 12: Record your results. How much gold did you recover? Did you lose any mercury? What could you improve? Remember: this exercise uses real mercury. Do not do it indoors. Do not let children watch. If you feel dizzy or have a headache, stop and get fresh air. Practice this exercise only under supervision if you are new. The goal is to learn the method while minimizing danger. In many African mining communities, you can practice with a local cooperative that has safety equipment. Always prioritize safety over speed.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Mercury Amalgamation in African Gold Processing

Mercury amalgamation remains one of the most widely usedâand most dangerousâmethods for recovering fine gold in artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) across Africa. From the ashanti goldfields of Ghana to the copper-gold belts of Zambia, the tin-gold regions of Nigeria, and the alluvial deposits of Tanzania and Zimbabwe, mercury is still used because it is cheap, portable, and effective at capturing free gold from concentrates. For the African agribusiness entrepreneur or processing cooperative, however, mercury is not just a technical inputâit is a liability, a regulatory risk, and a public health hazard that can destroy a business and a community.

This practical reference module is designed to give operators, trainers, and cooperative managers a business-first understanding of mercury amalgamation: what it is, how it is done, where it fails, and how to protect workers, communities, and commercial viability. It assumes you are already familiar with the step-by-step method covered in earlier lessons and now need a consolidated reference for field use, training, and decision-making.

Why Mercury Amalgamation Still Matters in African ASM

Mercury forms an alloyâan amalgamâwith gold when the two are brought into contact. The amalgam is then heated to evaporate the mercury, leaving behind a gold-mercury sponge that is further refined. In Africa, this method is used because:

  • Low capital requirement: A retort, a pan, and a few grams of mercury cost far less than a gravity separation plant or a cyanidation circuit.
  • Portability: Mercury can be carried to remote sites where electricity and water are unreliable.
  • Speed: A skilled operator can recover visible gold from a concentrate in under an hour.
  • Familiarity: Generations of miners have used mercury, creating a knowledge baseâand a false sense of safety.

But the business case is weakening. Mercury is toxic, increasingly regulated under the Minamata Convention on Mercury, and a growing number of buyersâincluding refiners in South Africa, the UAE, and Europeâare refusing mercury-contaminated gold. For African agribusinesses that process gold as a side enterprise or as a community service, the reputational and legal risks now outweigh the short-term convenience.

Data Table 1: Mercury Use and Losses in Selected African ASM Countries

Country Estimated ASM Gold Output (tonnes/year) Estimated Mercury Use (tonnes/year) Mercury Lost to Environment (%) Key Risk
Ghana ~30â50 ~20â30 70â80 Water contamination in Pra and Ankobra basins
Tanzania ~20â30 ~15â25 65â75 Soil and air contamination near Geita and Kahama
Zimbabwe ~15â25 ~10â20 60â75 Worker exposure in Kadoma and Shurugwi
Nigeria ~10â20 ~8â15 70â85 Lead-mercury co-exposure in Zamfara
Democratic Republic of Congo ~15â25 ~10â20 75â85 Riverine mercury in South Kivu and Ituri

Sources: UNEP Global Mercury Assessment (2018); Minamata Convention Secretariat, National Action Plans (various); African Mineral Development Centre, ASM Data Portal (2022). Figures are estimates and vary by season and gold price.

Data Table 2: Cost-Benefit Snapshot â Mercury vs. Mercury-Free Alternatives

Method Upfront Cost (USD) Recovery Rate (%) Health & Regulatory Risk Market Acceptance
Mercury amalgamation (uncontrolled) 50â200 40â60 Very High Low (buyers reject)
Mercury amalgamation with retort 200â800 50â70 High Medium
Gravity separation (shaking table) 1,500â5,000 60â80 Low High
Borax smelting 300â1,000 70â90 Low High

Sources: World Bank, Artisanal and Small-Scale Mining: A Review of the Issues (2020); UNEP, Reducing Mercury Use in ASM (2018); Global Environment Facility, Mercury-Free Gold Processing (2021). Costs are indicative and vary by country and scale.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Mercury Vapour Is Odourless, Invisible, and Deadly

Heating mercury amalgam in open air releases mercury vapour that can cause permanent brain damage, kidney failure, and death. Never burn amalgam indoors, near food, or without a retort. A single gram of mercury can contaminate a 20-acre lake. In African ASM communities, mercury poisoning often presents as tremors, memory loss, and kidney diseaseâsymptoms frequently misdiagnosed as malaria or stress. If you suspect mercury exposure, stop work immediately, move to fresh air, and seek medical attention. Report spills to local environmental authorities.

Quick Reference Checklist for Safe and Compliant Mercury Handling

  1. Use a retort: Always heat amalgam in a closed retort with a condenser. Never open-burn amalgam.
  2. Wear PPE: Nitrile gloves, goggles, and a respirator with mercury vapour cartridges. Change gloves after every session.
  3. Work outdoors or ventilated: Never handle mercury in enclosed rooms, kitchens, or near children.
  4. Store mercury safely: Keep in sealed, labelled, unbreakable containers away from heat and food.
  5. Capture spills: Use sulphur powder or zinc dust to bind spilled mercury; never vacuum or sweep dry.
  6. Monitor health: Annual urine mercury testing for all workers handling mercury.
  7. Document and report: Keep records of mercury purchased, used, and recovered. Report to national Minamata focal points.
  8. Plan transition: Set a business timeline to move to gravity, borax, or cyanidation alternatives within 12â24 months.

Business-First Considerations for African Operators

Mercury amalgamation is not just a technical choiceâit is a commercial one. Buyers in Johannesburg, Dubai, and Zurich are increasingly requiring mercury-free certification. Banks and development finance institutions are screening for environmental compliance. Insurance companies are refusing to cover mercury-related liabilities. For African agribusinesses that want to scale, the question is not whether to abandon mercury, but how quickly and at what cost.

The good news is that mercury-free alternatives are proven and increasingly affordable. Gravity separation using shaking tables and centrifuges works well for coarse gold. Borax smelting is a low-cost, low-toxicity method for fine gold. Cyanidation, when properly regulated, offers the highest recovery rates. Training programmes funded by the Global Environment Facility, UNEP, and the African Development Bank are available across Ghana, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe.

For cooperatives, the smart move is to phase out mercury while building a premium brand around responsible sourcing. Mercury-free gold can attract a price premium of 5â15% in ethical markets. That premium, combined with lower health costs and reduced regulatory risk, makes the transition a business caseânot just a moral one.

Further Reading (Free Official Links)

  • UNEP Global Mercury Assessment 2018 â authoritative data on mercury emissions and ASM.
  • Minamata Convention on Mercury â official treaty text, national action plans, and guidance.
  • World Bank ASM Review â economic and policy analysis for African ASM.
  • Artisanal Gold Council â mercury-free processing guides and training materials.
  • UNEP Mercury Programme â tools, case studies, and regional reports for Africa.

Prepared for Rise AFRICA Skills â Gold Smelting and Refining. This module is for training purposes and does not replace national regulations or professional medical advice. Always consult your country's environmental and mining authorities before handling mercury.

quiz.q: What is the main reason mercury is used in small-scale gold mining?
options: A) It is cheap and captures fine gold
C) It is safe for the environment
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Mercury is popular because it is inexpensive and effectively binds with fine gold particles.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a health effect of mercury poisoning?
quiz.explanation: Mercury attacks the nervous system, kidneys, and lungs, causing serious health problems.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ratio of mercury to expected gold by weight?
quiz.explanation: A 1:1 ratio ensures enough mercury to capture gold without making the amalgam too runny.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using aluminum containers for mercury?
quiz.explanation: Mercury forms an amalgam with aluminum, damaging the container and contaminating the mercury.

quiz.q: What type of gloves should you wear when handling mercury?
quiz.explanation: Nitrile gloves resist mercury penetration, while latex gloves allow mercury to pass through.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a retort in amalgamation?
quiz.explanation: A retort captures mercury vapor during burning, allowing it to be reused and preventing pollution.

quiz.q: How long should you stir the mercury and concentrate together?
quiz.explanation: Stirring for 15â20 minutes ensures mercury contacts all gold particles.

quiz.q: What should you do if you spill mercury?
options: C) Wash it down the drain
quiz.explanation: Sulfur binds with mercury to form a less dangerous compound that can be swept up safely.

quiz.q: Why is burning amalgam the most dangerous step?
options: A) It releases toxic mercury vapor
B) It can cause a fire
quiz.explanation: Burning amalgam releases mercury as an invisible, highly toxic vapor that can be inhaled.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when using mercury?
quiz.explanation: Using too much mercury makes the amalgam runny and difficult to squeeze, leading to gold loss.

quiz.q: How should you store mercury?
options: B) In a sealed glass or plastic container
quiz.explanation: Mercury evaporates at room temperature, so it must be stored in a sealed container.

quiz.q: What is methylmercury?
options: B) A less toxic form of mercury
C) A highly toxic form that builds up in fish
D) A mercury compound used in mining
quiz.explanation: Bacteria in water convert mercury to methylmercury, which accumulates in fish and can poison people who eat them.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid eating fish from waters contaminated with mercury?
quiz.explanation: Methylmercury builds up in fish tissues and can cause mercury poisoning in humans.

quiz.q: What should you do after handling mercury?
options: B) Wash hands and face with soap
quiz.explanation: Washing thoroughly removes any mercury residue and prevents ingestion.

quiz.q: What is a safer alternative to mercury amalgamation?
quiz.explanation: Gravity separation methods like panning or sluicing capture gold without toxic chemicals.

quiz.q: How can you tell if someone has mercury poisoning?
options: B) They have tremors and memory loss
quiz.explanation: Neurological symptoms like tremors, memory problems, and mouth sores are signs of mercury poisoning.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the amalgamation process?
quiz.explanation: Concentrating the gold by panning or sluicing removes dirt and improves mercury contact.

quiz.q: Why is it important to work outdoors when using mercury?
options: B) To avoid accumulating toxic vapors
quiz.explanation: Outdoor work allows mercury vapor to disperse, reducing inhalation risk.

quiz.q: What should you do with excess mercury after squeezing the amalgam?
options: C) Pour it down the sink
quiz.explanation: Mercury can be filtered and reused, saving money and reducing waste.

quiz.q: What is a retort made of?
quiz.explanation: A retort typically consists of a metal pipe and a condenser to capture mercury vapor.

quiz.q: How much mercury is typically used for 5 grams of gold?
quiz.explanation: A 1:1 ratio means 5 grams of mercury for 5 grams of expected gold.

quiz.q: What is the danger of using a vacuum cleaner on a mercury spill?
quiz.explanation: Vacuuming disperses mercury into the air as vapor, increasing inhalation risk.

quiz.q: Why should pregnant women avoid mercury exposure?
options: B) It can harm the unborn baby
quiz.explanation: Mercury can cross the placenta and damage the developing nervous system of the fetus.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to dispose of mercury waste?
options: C) Take to a hazardous waste facility
quiz.explanation: Mercury waste must be handled by proper hazardous waste facilities to prevent environmental contamination.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel dizzy while working with mercury?
options: B) Stop and get fresh air
quiz.explanation: Dizziness is a sign of mercury vapor inhalation; stop immediately and move to fresh air.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of using a plastic sheet under your work area?
quiz.explanation: A plastic sheet contains any mercury spills, making cleanup easier and safer.

quiz.q: How can you test if your mercury is dirty?
quiz.explanation: Dirty mercury often appears dull or black due to oxidation and contaminants.

quiz.q: What is the final product after burning the amalgam?
quiz.explanation: Burning evaporates the mercury, leaving a gold button that can be melted further.

quiz.q: Why is it important to educate your family about mercury dangers?
options: B) To make them work faster
quiz.explanation: Family members, especially children, can be exposed to mercury if not properly informed.

quiz.q: What is a spill kit for mercury made of?
options: B) Sulfur powder and a sealed container
quiz.explanation: Sulfur powder binds mercury, and a sealed container holds the waste safely.
